newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Gasoline futures fizzles as speculators flee.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Gasoline futures fizzles as speculators flee.

text.p: A speculative bubble burst in the August gasoline futures on the contract expiry day Thursday, putting the brakes on a crude oil rally and leaving traders nervous about the next big move for prices.
"The bubble in gasoline burst. The expiry of the August contract leaves us with the autumn months when demand for gasoline typically falls," said John Saucer, analyst with Smith Barney in Houston.

August gasoline ended off 2.06 cents at 67.84 cents a gallon. Speculators dumped the contract after bidding it up more than ten cents since last Wednesday in a bet that tightening gasoline supplies and strong demand would keep prices firm.
"A lot of the speculative interest we saw was pent up," said Pat Hughes, market analyst with Chevron Corp in Walnut Creek, California.

"Many people had turned bearish on oil prices in the second quarter due to the expected restart of Iraq oil sales. Then gasoline demand had become so exceptional that speculators could no longer ignore it," said Hughes.

Data released by the American Petroleum Institute (API) have showed feverish 8.7 million-barrel-per-day (bpd) "implied demand" for gasoline over the past month. (Implied demand is an estimate based on stocks movement, imports and production).

Demand has gobbled up refiner stocks of so-called reformulated gasoline (RFG), which meets tough Environmental Protection Agency standards and is the only grade deliverable against the NYMEX futures contract.
Meanwhile, Tosco Corp shut down a gasoline making unit at its Bayway, New Jersey refinery on Wednesday after detecting a leak. The unit is the largest of its kind in the world.
Another kicker came from the temporary closure of Exxon's Baytown, Texas gas-making unit after a lightnening strike. That unit is almost as large as Tosco's.
According to some traders, tight supplies could continue into next month, even though gasoline demand historically peaks around the July 4 weekend.

"Even after the August expiry, There are clearly some who think that the rash of refinery problems will continue the uptrend for gasoline," said Gerald Samuels, managing director of ARB Oil in New York.
However, analysts said a variety of other factors may conspire to undermine gasoline prices and the oil complex in general.

"The high gasoline prices here are going to attract cargoes from all over the place, and the high crack spreads are going to encourage refiners to maintain a high level of gasoline production," said Smith Barney's Saucer, noting supply tightness may be a very temporary phenomenon.

After dragging its heels for two months since the United Nations allowed it a second $2 billion round of oil-for-aid sales, Iraq has finally put all the pieces in place to resume its exports and should be ready to export as early as next week.

Given the delay in restarting and the requirement that Iraq sells around $1 billion of oil by September 5 or forego some of its allowance, it may be pumping oil out onto the market at a very high rate, depressing prices sharply, analyst said.
